findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Treasury Management Quarter 1 Update 2026-27
findings.headline: Financing costs as proportion of revenue forecast to grow from 19% to 26% by 2028/29, reducing financial flexibility
findings.detail: Interest payable and Minimum Revenue Provision on borrowing consumed 18% of net revenue stream in 2025/26, 19% in Q1 2026/27, with budgeted growth to 25% for full year 2026/27 and 26% by 2028/29. This upward trajectory reflects the Council's shift from using capital receipts (North Weald airfield sale proceeds) to PWLB borrowing to fund the capital programme. As a proportion approaches one quarter of revenue, flexibility for responding to unexpected pressures or service investment diminishes.
findings.matters: For a lender, rising financing costs as a proportion of revenue indicate declining financial headroom. At 26% of revenue, the council is approaching levels where service spending and investment become constrained by debt servicing obligations.
findings.quote: Proportion of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream (Standard CIPFA Indicator) 18% 19% 25%* 26%* 26%*

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Treasury Management Quarter 1 Update 2026-27
findings.headline: £30 million commercial loan to Qualis maturing September 2030 creates refinancing risk in less than four years
findings.detail: The Council lent £30 million to Qualis (a wholly owned subsidiary) for commercial property investments as a 10-year maturity loan with principal due September 2030. This represents a material refinancing requirement coming due in 48 months, secured only by a floating charge over Qualis' assets. Given the £30 million concentration, refinancing conditions at that time will materially affect the Council's debt costs.
findings.matters: A single £30 million refinancing event within four years creates concentration and timing risk. If Qualis property investments underperform or credit conditions tighten, refinancing could be difficult or expensive, forcing early repayment or drawdown of reserves.
findings.figures: £30,000,000 outstanding balance as at 30 June 2026; maturity September 2030; 10-year loan granted September 2020
findings.quote: The Commercial Loan with Qualis had an outstanding balance of £30.0 million as at 30 June 2026 and is presented in Table 7 below.

findings.headline: Borrowing increased by £24.7m to £262.3m during 2025/26 to support capital projects
findings.detail: Treasury management end-of-year report shows borrowing increased by £24.7 million to £262.3 million. Capital expenditure totalled £58.6 million and capital financial requirement stood at £346.3 million.
findings.matters: Material increase in absolute borrowing affects debt profile and financial position; lenders need to understand the council's borrowing trajectory and the capital projects being financed.
findings.figures: Borrowing increased by £24.7 million to £262.3 million; capital expenditure £58.6 million; capital financial requirement £346.3 million
findings.quote: borrowing had increased by £24.7 million to £262.3 million this supported support capital projects

findings.headline: Qualis subsidiary company risks highlighted throughout external audit assessment of value for money and financial statements
findings.detail: The external auditor's planning report references Qualis (the council's development company) throughout as a material area impacting both Value for Money and financial statement audits, with EY to present a summary of Qualis-related issues to the committee.
findings.matters: Subsidiary company activities and risks directly affect group financial statements and audit scope; Qualis's ongoing risks and development timeline are material considerations for lenders assessing financial position.
findings.figures: Qualis development completion estimated for financial year 2026/27
findings.quote: References to Qualis were shown in different parts of the audit plan as this impacted on VfM and the financial statement audits. EY would look to present a summary of issues related to Qualis to the next committee

findings.headline: Planning performance risk has crystallised on the risk register
findings.detail: The Strategic Director reported that the planning performance risk had crystallised, indicating that a previously anticipated operational risk has now materialised and will remain under review.
findings.matters: Planning fee income is a material revenue stream; degraded planning performance affects both fee income and service delivery, and materialized risks suggest management or resource constraints.
findings.quote: The planning performance risk had crystallised, the risk would be reviewed and remain on the risk register

findings.headline: Commercial property rental issues under active review with audit recommendations being implemented
findings.detail: Committee members raised concerns about commercial rents; officers confirmed that improvement work is underway and audit recommendations related to this area are being monitored.
findings.matters: Revenue from commercial property is important to financial sustainability; active concerns and ongoing improvement work suggest management or operational issues requiring resolution.
findings.quote: Concerns were raised about commercial rents, officers confirmed improvement work was underway and the audit recommendations are being monitored

findings.headline: Internal Audit explicitly identifies financial sustainability as main risk for 2026/27
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit's annual report identified financial sustainability, alongside LGR, cyber security, data protection, and staffing, as the main risks facing the council in the coming year.
findings.matters: The council's own internal audit function has flagged financial sustainability as a material forward-looking risk—a direct signal that the council recognizes affordability pressures ahead.
findings.quote: Internal Audit had identified financial sustainability, Local Government Reorganisation (LGR), cyber security, data protection, and staffing as the main risks for 2026/27

findings.headline: Finance team facing capacity and capability challenges being factored into audit planning
findings.detail: External auditors and the council agreed to work together to support the audit, with explicit note that the finance team has a range of challenges and the capacity of the team would be considered in planning.
findings.matters: Finance team capacity directly affects the council's ability to produce quality financial reporting, manage budgets, and provide financial oversight—all critical to financial sustainability.
findings.quote: the finance team did have a range of challenges and the capacity of the team would be considered

findings.headline: External auditor reports work continuing to rebuild audit assurance from prior years
findings.detail: The 2025/26 external audit planning report notes that work was continuing to rebuild audit assurance, indicating prior-year audit findings or control gaps. The committee stressed the importance of rebuilding assurance from previous years.
findings.matters: Prior audit weaknesses suggest control or governance gaps that could affect financial reporting quality and the council's ability to manage finances effectively.
findings.quote: work was continuing to rebuild audit assurance, and stressed the importance of completing the planned work for 2025/26

findings.headline: Balance sheet resources forecast to decline from £68.1m to £42.2m over two years
findings.detail: According to the Liability Benchmark table, usable reserves (Balance Sheet resources) are forecast to fall from £68.109m at 31/03/26 to £39.5m (2027) and £42.2m (2028). This reflects ongoing deployment of reserves to fund capital activity, reducing the council's financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce a council's ability to absorb shocks, manage timing mismatches, or fund emergency capital needs. Lower reserves also signal reliance on sustained borrowing.
findings.figures: Balance Sheet resources: £68.109m (2026), £45.5m forecast (2026), £39.5m forecast (2027), £42.2m forecast (2028)
findings.quote: Less: Balance Sheet resources (116.4) (45.5) (39.5) (42.2)

findings.headline: £30m Qualis commercial loan carries no Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP), deferring repayment until September 2030
findings.detail: The council granted a 10-year maturity loan to Qualis in September 2020 with no principal repayment until maturity in 2030. Under accounting rules at the time, MRP was not required. The council has protected itself with a floating charge on underlying commercial assets, but principal repayment is deferred a full decade.
findings.matters: A lender reviewing debt sustainability needs to know that £30m of borrowing is entirely unamortised until 2030. If Qualis assets underperform or the council's finances deteriorate, there is no contractual mechanism to recover principal earlier.
findings.figures: Qualis Investment Loan: £30.0m; maturity September 2030; no MRP charged
findings.quote: Members should note that, in accordance with the Council's MRP Policy and the prevailing accounting rules at the point at which the Commercial Loan to Qualis was granted (in September 2020), MRP is not provided on this loan.

findings.headline: Qualis subsidiary lending has grown to £87.95m; development loans increased £9.1m in one year
findings.detail: Service loans to Qualis (the council's property development subsidiary) total £87.95m as at 31 March 2026. Development loans alone increased by £9.142m to £44.702m during the year to support Springwood Grove project completion. Combined with a £30m commercial loan, total Qualis exposure is £117.95m.
findings.matters: Lending to subsidiaries is riskier than traditional capital investment and concentration risk on a single entity. If Springwood Grove underperforms, the council cannot recover these funds or charge them to service budgets; they sit as loan assets on the balance sheet.
findings.figures: Development loans to Qualis: £44.702m (increase of £9.142m); total Service Investment loans £87.95m; Qualis Commercial Loan £30.0m
findings.quote: Outstanding Developments Loans to Qualis have increased by £9.142 million during the year; this enabled the continued development of Springwood Grove.

findings.headline: Capital receipts of £83.9m (North Weald Airfield sale) have been fully deployed; council now dependent on PWLB borrowing
findings.detail: In 2025/26, the council applied £83.948m of capital receipts to its capital programme, compared to £13.968m the prior year. This represents the drawdown of the major North Weald Airfield capital receipt received in December 2023. The council has now moved from being able to self-fund capital activity to accessing PWLB loans, a structural shift in its financing profile.
findings.matters: Large one-off receipts can mask underlying financing weakness. Once exhausted, a council that cannot self-fund capital must borrow continuously. This changes risk profile and debt sustainability analysis.
findings.figures: Capital receipts applied: £83.948m (2025/26) vs £13.968m (2024/25); North Weald receipt received December 2023
findings.quote: The Council is now accessing loan finance through PWLB following the use of the funds.

findings.headline: Commercial property income fell by £0.98m, the largest decline in the portfolio
findings.detail: Net income from commercial property investments dropped from £8.935m (2024/25) to £7.954m (2025/26). The council attributes this to a vacancy in the 'Other' category (which includes North Weald Airfield), forcing the council to pay Non-Domestic Rates rather than receiving rent. The portfolio's £182.5m valuation may be at risk if vacancy rates persist.
findings.matters: Commercial property is the council's largest income stream and a key revenue generator. A decline signals either asset quality issues or market weakness, both of which affect debt servicing capacity.
findings.figures: Commercial property net income fell from £8.935m to £7.954m; portfolio value £182.539m; 'Other' income fell from £0.998m to -£0.029m
findings.quote: Other commercial income reduced due to a vacancy and hence Non-Domestic rates have become payable by the Council.

findings.headline: External borrowing increased by £24.7m in a single year, with more increases forecast
findings.detail: The council's external borrowing rose from £253.2m to £277.9m during 2025/26. More significantly, the Liability Benchmark forecast shows the council will need to borrow an additional £53m over the next two years (from £299.9m at end 2026 to £346.6m forecast for end 2028), driven by capital programme commitments and depletion of reserves.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand debt trajectory and whether the council's capital plans are sustainable. The shift from one-off capital receipts to sustained external borrowing signals a structural change in funding sources.
findings.figures: Borrowing increased £24.7m to £277.9m; Liability Benchmark £299.9m (2026), £331.0m (2027), £346.6m (2028)
findings.quote: Borrowing – external borrowing increased by £24.7 million (from £253.2 million to £277.9 million) during the period April 2025 to March 2026

findings.headline: Social Housing Regulator inspection expected 26/27 with risk of fines and enforcement
findings.detail: The council must now comply with the Social Housing (Regulation) Act 2023 and Consumer Standards. A regulator inspection is expected in 26/27. While the council has implemented compliance systems and completed self-assessment, the register identifies weak areas in ASB handling and complaints management. Enforcement action could result in fines and loss of operating authority.
findings.matters: As a significant housing provider, regulatory fines or loss of social housing control would directly impact finances and operations.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this document
findings.quote: Failure to meet Consumer Standards in the Social Housing (Regulation) Act (2023) could result in reputational damage, financial impact and fines

findings.headline: Unprecedented surge in homelessness creating immediate financial pressure on general fund
findings.detail: The council has seen an unprecedented increase in homeless households due to national factors including the cost of living crisis and the Domestic Abuse Act. There is additional risk from bridging hotels in the district and asylum seekers. While the council has received additional government funding and agreed block booking arrangements, the costs are immediate and ongoing and add pressure to an already-stressed general fund.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation costs are a direct drain on the general fund and are difficult to control when driven by national factors beyond the council's influence.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this document
findings.quote: We have seen an unprecedented increase in households becoming homeless due to national factors (cost of living and the implications of the Domestic Abuse Act). There is a possible additional risk of increasing numbers locally from the bridging hotels (2 in the district) if they are made to leave without arrangements for rehousing elsewhere being in place.

findings.headline: Qualis LATCO facing viability pressure from interest rate rises on development schemes
findings.detail: The council's LATCO (Qualis Group) is operating in difficult economic conditions, with sharp interest rate increases now threatening the viability of planned housing and regeneration schemes. The council's medium-term income projections depend entirely on Qualis delivering these schemes successfully and on the margins generated through on-lending. A failure to maintain viability would create significant financial loss to the council at a time when the general fund is already in deficit.
findings.matters: The council relies on Qualis returns for income. A major LATCO failure would directly worsen the budget gap and trigger additional savings needs.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this document
findings.quote: The Council's LATCO, the Qualis Group, has had to operate in particularly difficult economic and trading conditions since its inception. This is proving challenging in property development especially, with the recent sharp increase in worldwide interest rates threatening the viability of planned housing and regeneration schemes. In particular, the Council's medium-term income assumptions are dependent on the successful delivery of these schemes through the margins that it makes on on-lending to Qualis.

findings.headline: General Fund budget gap of £3.261m for 2026/27 with structural deficit of £5.2m by 2030
findings.detail: The updated MTFP approved in February 2025 shows a £3.261m budget gap for the coming financial year and a structural deficit of £5.2m by 2030. The council's ability to close these gaps depends significantly on the North Weald Airfield capital receipt; the register notes that applying the receipt would worsen the base budget gap, leaving the council dependent on a sale that may not deliver as expected. Savings identification is still ongoing.
findings.matters: The council has a legal duty to maintain a balanced budget. A structural deficit of this scale signals underlying financial stress that will require either sustained savings delivery or reserve drawdown.
findings.figures: £3.261m budget gap 2026/27; £5.2m structural deficit by 31/03/30
findings.quote: The updated Medium-Term Financial Plan (MTFP) 2025/26 to 2029/30 approved by Full Council on 20th February 2025 showed a General Fund budget gap of £3.261 million for 2026/27 with a longer-term structural deficit of £5.2 million by 31/03/30. However, the forecast also assumes that the North Weald Airfield capital receipt is locked in (with the Council dependent on the interest generated) i.e. application of the receipt would worsen the base budget gap.

findings.paper_title: EFDC Annual Governance Statement 25_26 covering report
findings.headline: Senior Leadership Team was not actively monitoring balance sheet risks in 2024/25
findings.detail: The Council's previous governance review identified that balance sheet risks were not receiving active SLT oversight, creating a significant risk to financial sustainability. The remedy is to present the balance sheet as at 31st March 2026 to SLT for discussion by 31 August 2026 — meaning the action is imminent as of this document.
findings.matters: A lender depends on balance sheet risks being actively managed; if they remain hidden until they become budget issues, a council's financial position can deteriorate rapidly without warning.
findings.figures: 31 August 2026 target date
findings.quote: Without active SLT oversight, balance sheet risks stay hidden until they become budget issues. With effective SLT monitoring, they become manageable, informed strategic decisions.

findings.headline: Newly introduced debt write-off process contained weaknesses identified through detailed testing
findings.detail: A review of the council's debt write-off process (which appears to be newly established) was undertaken to give the Section 151 Officer assurance. Testing identified areas for further improvement, suggesting the process is not yet fully effective.
findings.matters: Debt write-off controls affect the accuracy of income accounting and bad-debt provisioning; weaknesses could indicate financial statements risk or that the council is not recovering debts effectively
findings.figures: Not specified in document
findings.quote: Areas for further improvement were highlighted by Internal Audit following detailed testing

findings.headline: Council had compliance gap with Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 and required remedial action plan
findings.detail: The Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 introduced in September 2025 a new offence holding organisations accountable if they fail to prevent fraud by employees where reasonable safeguards are not in place. Following a gap analysis, Internal Audit developed an action plan to ensure the council meets the new legal requirements and is overseeing its implementation.
findings.matters: Compliance failure with anti-fraud legislation creates both legal risk and control risk; identifies that the council's governance framework was not proactively updated when legislation changed
findings.figures: No specific figures; legislation came into effect September 2025
findings.quote: Following a gap analysis, Internal Audit has developed an action plan and is overseeing its implementation.

findings.headline: Housing contractor procurement did not follow formal tendering process; supplier spend lacked monitoring controls
findings.detail: Internal Audit investigation found that procurement processes were not fully followed for a housing contractor engagement. A formal tender and contract should have been in place, and supplier spending was not properly monitored to ensure compliance. The finding indicates a breakdown in standard procurement controls for what appears to be a material contract.
findings.matters: Procurement control failures create financial risk; without formal tenders and monitoring, the council may not achieve value for money and could overpay suppliers, directly affecting financial position
findings.figures: Not specified in document
findings.quote: Procurement processes were not fully followed. A formal tender and contract should have been in place, and supplier spend needs better monitoring to ensure compliance and timely contract establishment.

findings.headline: Two audit areas received Limited Assurance ratings: tree strategy and commercial rents
findings.detail: Of ten audit reviews completed, six received Substantial Assurance and two Reasonable, but two received Limited Assurance. Limited Assurance means 'significant gaps, weaknesses or non-compliance were identified' requiring improvement to the system of governance, risk management and control.
findings.matters: Limited Assurance on commercial rents is material to a lender assessing the council's income management and asset control; both findings indicate the council has identified areas where its control systems need strengthening
findings.figures: 2 Limited Assurance ratings out of 10 audits completed; 6 Substantial, 2 Reasonable, 0 No Assurance
findings.quote: The two limited assurance reports relate to tree strategy and commercial rents.

findings.headline: EPR grant funding volatility creating significant forecasting instability
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) grant volatility as creating 'significant instability within the forecasting process.' Core funding is flat for two years while this discretionary grant remains unpredictable, forcing reliance on conservative forecasting assumptions that may not hold.
findings.matters: Volatile and unpredictable funding sources undermine medium-term financial planning; a lender needs confidence in predictable revenue streams, not reliance on contingency reserves to cover forecast miss
findings.figures: EPR income was £0.3m higher than budgeted in 2025-26; MTFP reflects forecast reductions; flat core funding 2027/28 and 2028/29
findings.quote: At the same time, the Council continues to face volatility in other key income streams, specifically the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) grant, leaving significant instability within the forecasting process.

findings.headline: External audit costs overrunning by £0.15m as newly appointed firm rebuilds audit assurance
findings.detail: External audit costs were £0.15m above budget for the 2024/25 audit, attributed to 'additional work required for the 2024/25 audit by the newly appointed audit firm, as part of the ongoing rebuild of audit assurance.' This language suggests prior audit issues or control weaknesses that the new firm is investigating.
findings.matters: A newly appointed auditor requiring additional scope hours to 'rebuild' audit assurance suggests prior control deficiencies or matters of concern that needed deeper investigation
findings.figures: £0.15m audit costs above budget in 2025-26
findings.quote: External audit costs of £0.15 million above budget, relating to additional work required for the 2024/25 audit by the newly appointed audit firm, as part of the ongoing rebuild of audit assurance.

findings.headline: Bad debt provision increase of £0.40m due to long-standing commercial debts collection issues
findings.detail: The council reviewed its bad debt provision methodology and increased the allocation by £0.40m to 'more closely reflect the recovery position of long standing commercial debts.' This suggests material debts that have not been collected despite historical efforts.
findings.matters: Persistent commercial debt collection issues indicate operational or contractual problems with major debtors that may signal broader commercial relationships under stress
findings.figures: £0.40m additional bad debt provision in 2025-26
findings.quote: The bad debt provision methodology has been reviewed, resulting in an additional allocation of £0.40m to more closely reflect the recovery position of long standing commercial debts.

findings.headline: Unbudgeted Bell Hotel legal costs of £0.86m for single year
findings.detail: The council incurred £0.86m in unbudgeted legal fees related to the Bell Hotel. While described as non-recurrent, this represents a material contingent liability exposure that materialised unforecast and demonstrates the council's exposure to unexpected legal costs.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted legal costs of this scale indicate either weak horizon scanning or inherent exposure to property/asset-related disputes that may recur
findings.figures: £0.86m legal fees in relation to the Bell Hotel in 2025-26
findings.quote: The outturn reflects legal costs of £0.86m, in relation to the Bell Hotel. This expenditure was unbudgeted, but as non-recurrent, will not be required in future years.

findings.headline: Housing acquisitions programme viability reassessed downward by £3.29m due to market factors
findings.detail: Housing acquisitions budget of £8.75m underspent by £3.29m after 'financial viability reassessments on some sites in the light of changing market factors.' This suggests assumptions about property costs or project economics were overstated, affecting the capital programme profile.
findings.matters: Market-driven revaluations of scheme viability may indicate property market weakness or cost inflation that affects the broader capital programme and asset strategy
findings.figures: Housing Acquisitions budget £8.75m, outturn £5.46m, underspend £3.29m
findings.quote: Housing Acquisitions, which had a budget of £8.75m in 2025/26, has an outturn of £5.46m. The underspend of £3.29m is due to financial viability reassessments on some sites in the light of changing market factors.

findings.headline: Housebuilding programme delayed by planning issues with £12.14m underspend and schemes now expected in 2026/27
findings.detail: The HRA housebuilding budget of £12.42m resulted in only £0.28m spend in 2025-26 due to planning delays. Major schemes including St Peters Avenue (£6.50m), Chequers B Site (£1.81m), and former Princess of Wales Public House (£1.65m) are now expected to commence in 2026/27. This reflects delivery challenges on strategic housing development.
findings.matters: Housing supply is a corporate priority and lender concern; serial delays indicate either weak project management or unrealistic planning timescales, both of which raise delivery risk on other council schemes
findings.figures: Housebuilding budget £12.42m, actual spend £0.28m, underspend £12.14m; St Peters Avenue (£6.50m), Chequers B (£1.81m), Princess of Wales (£1.65m) expected 2026/27
findings.quote: A number of schemes have encountered planning issues and delays, with only minor spend on professional fees taking place during the year. The schemes are expected to commence during 2026/27 and include major schemes at St Peters Avenue (£6.50m), Chequers B Site (£1.81m), and the former Princess of Wales Public House (£1.65m).

findings.headline: Medium-term funding gaps of £1.54m and £2.69m in 2027/28 and 2028/29 with core funding flat
findings.detail: Despite a balanced 2026/27 budget, the approved MTFP shows deficits of £1.54m in 2027/28 and £2.69m in 2028/29. The government's three-year settlement confirms core funding will be largely flat in outer years. The council notes the MTFP 'assumes an increase in reserves' to manage these gaps, indicating reliance on one-time resources rather than structural solutions.
findings.matters: Unresolved structural deficits require service reductions or further savings plans; reliance on reserve drawdown is not a sustainable long-term strategy and limits financial resilience
findings.figures: £1.54m deficit 2027/28; £2.69m deficit 2028/29; approved MTFP assumes increase in reserves reflecting underspend and budgeted contributions of £1.47m
findings.quote: While the budget for 2026/27 has been balanced, there remains a deficit in future years of £1.54m in 2027/28 and £2.69m in 2028/29. At the same time, the Council continues to face volatility in other key income streams, specifically the Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) grant, leaving significant instability within the forecasting process.

findings.headline: Dry recyclables market volatility creating £0.88m budget pressure outside council control
findings.detail: The cost of processing dry recyclables and sales income are affected by global market changes with volatile rates outside council control. Budgeted income was set on average prices over three years, which were much higher than current rates. The MTFP has been adjusted to reflect this as a recurring budget pressure.
findings.matters: This exposes the council to commodity price volatility and indicates an income assumption that cannot be relied upon in future years
findings.figures: £0.88m overspend on net cost of managing dry recyclables in 2025-26
findings.quote: The cost of and sales income from processing dry recyclables is affected by global market changes, with rates being volatile and outside of Council control. The budgeted income was set with regard to average sales prices over the last 3 years. This was much higher than current rates. The MTFP has been adjusted to reflect this budget pressure.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand surging at 47% year-on-year with no short-term solution
findings.detail: The number of households in temporary accommodation rose from 117 to 172 between March 2025 and March 2026, driving a £0.52m B&B overspend. The council acknowledges this cannot be managed through short-term mitigations alone and has commissioned a Temporary Accommodation Options Appraisal to increase capacity and reduce reliance on expensive nightly-paid accommodation. This sustained pressure will continue into future budgets.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can absorb and manage this demand-driven cost exposure, and whether the planned solutions will be sufficient to prevent compounding budget pressures
findings.figures: 117 households (March 2025) to 172 (March 2026); £0.52m overspend in 2025-26; approved MTFP for 2026/27-2028/29 makes provision for continuing pressures
findings.quote: The number of households placed in temporary accommodation (TA) rose from 117 at March 2025 to 172 at March 2026. This represents a year-on-year increase of approximately 47%. Addressing Homelessness demand will continue to be a key feature in managing budgets in 2026-27.

findings.paper_title: v1 Appendix B - EFDC Final Annual Auditors Report
findings.headline: Material misstatements were identified in 2024/25 accounts; some corrected, others left uncorrected by management
findings.detail: The auditor identified a number of material misstatements during the audit. While management corrected some, others were deliberately left in the financial statements. Separately, a large number of disclosure misstatements were also found. This indicates either control gaps in account preparation or deliberate acceptance of error.
findings.matters: Uncorrected material misstatements mean the financial statements are known to contain errors. A lender cannot rely on published figures and management may not be exercising robust oversight of accounting quality.
findings.figures: Material misstatements identified; volume described as requiring improvement; separate issue of large number of disclosure misstatements
findings.quote: A number of material misstatements were detected as a result of our work, some of which have been corrected whilst management has determined that others will remain uncorrected.

findings.paper_title: v1 Appendix B - EFDC Final Annual Auditors Report
findings.headline: Finance team capacity constraints caused a two-week pause to the audit and delays in delivering working papers
findings.detail: The audit had to pause for two weeks in November because the finance team lacked capacity to support the audit timetable. Working paper requests sent in June 2025 with a September deadline saw 'a sizeable portion' not responded to on time, creating a backlog that delayed the entire audit. Quality issues included hardcoded numbers instead of formulas in spreadsheets.
findings.matters: A council that cannot support an audit efficiently will struggle to operate effective financial controls. Staffing constraints in finance suggest vulnerability to error, fraud, and mismanagement.
findings.figures: Two-week audit pause due to finance team capacity; working paper requests sent 27 June 2025 with 26 September due date; audit restarted late November
findings.quote: A lack of capacity in the finance team has caused challenges in supporting the audit to the level required given the timeframe for the audit. This resulted in a two week pause to the year-end audit (which resumed in late November).

findings.paper_title: v1 Appendix B - EFDC Final Annual Auditors Report
findings.headline: Auditor unable to complete planned procedures on property valuations, IFRS 16 leases, and Qualis loan recoverability due to time constraints and incomplete evidence
findings.detail: EY was unable to conclude audit work on: valuation of land and buildings (pushed to late audit stages, then insufficient time to complete follow-up); IFRS 16 lease accounting (Council did not provide required lease contracts); and recoverability of Qualis loans (Council did not provide expected quality of working papers). These gaps contributed to the disclaimed opinion.
findings.matters: The council's balance sheet includes unaudited asset valuations and loan valuations. The auditor cannot confirm whether property assets are fairly stated or whether the Qualis loans represent a bigger loss than recorded.
findings.figures: Three significant audit areas with incomplete procedures; Qualis loan balance £81 million (unaudited for recoverability)
findings.quote: Due to delays in the audit timetable, our planned work on IFRS 16 implementation was rescheduled to the later stages of the audit. For the samples selected, the Council did not provide the required underlying lease contracts. Following our review of the information that was provided, additional follow-up evidence was required from the Council in order for us to conclude on this area. However, given the time constraints at this stage of the audit and the outstanding information, we were unable to complete the planned IFRS 16 procedures.

findings.paper_title: v1 Appendix B - EFDC Final Annual Auditors Report
findings.headline: MTFP projects deficits of £3.261m in 2026/27, requiring reserve drawdown across the forecast period
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Plan shows structural budget gaps every year from 2026/27 to 2029/30. The 2025/26 budget was only balanced through reduced reserve contributions and one-off adjustments. The council holds £7.931m in earmarked reserves and £4m minimum uncommitted reserve, but the MTFP assumes no further contributions — meaning reserves will be drawn as deficits emerge. By 2029/30 the annual deficit is £781k, cumulative gap by 2028/29 is £4.419m.
findings.matters: The council is on a declining reserve trajectory. Once reserves are depleted, it cannot continue to deliver current services without further borrowing or service reductions. This is a multi-year sustainability issue.
findings.figures: £3.261 million deficit 2026/27; cumulative £4.419 million gap by 2028/29; £7.931 million earmarked reserves; £4 million minimum General Fund reserve
findings.quote: However, future years show projected deficits of £3.261 million in 2026/27, decreasing to £781,000 by 2029/30.

findings.paper_title: v1 Appendix B - EFDC Final Annual Auditors Report
findings.headline: Planned savings of £3.536m for 2024/25 were not achieved; outturn relied on one-off underspends not recurring savings
findings.detail: The council's budget was built on £3.536m of permanent savings, but these did not materialise. The council reported an overall underspend only because of one-off benefits: project delays, staffing vacancies, and additional income. These cannot be repeated. The auditor notes that savings initiatives 'proved difficult to implement within the planned timeframe due to operational complexities' and service transformation was delayed.
findings.matters: The council's path to balanced budgets is not based on deliverable operational changes. If recurring savings cannot be achieved, the council will face structural deficits from 2026/27 onwards and will be forced to draw reserves faster than planned.
findings.figures: £3.536 million in planned savings for 2024/25; overall General Fund underspend of £775 million but driven by one-off factors (e.g., ICT/Transformation underspend of £1.123m due to delayed projects)
findings.quote: However, these planned savings were not fully achieved during the year. Instead, the Council's favourable outturn was largely the result of one-off underspends, such as project delays, staff vacancies and additional income, rather than the delivery of the targeted, recurring savings.

findings.paper_title: v1 Appendix B - EFDC Final Annual Auditors Report
findings.headline: Qualis Group subsidiary has £81m in outstanding council loans against only £61m in assets, with a £16m loan write-off planned for 2027/28
findings.detail: Epping Forest's wholly owned commercial subsidiary Qualis continues to experience ongoing trading losses and project delays. The expected credit loss on council loans jumped from £2m to £5m in 2024/25. An independent financial advisor has concluded that a £16m loan forgiveness is needed in 2027/28 to allow Qualis to operate at breakeven and begin repaying remaining debt. The council's investment in a Qualis carpark was written down from £19.4m in loan forgiveness to £3.4m asset value.
findings.matters: The council is exposed to a potential £16m loss on its own books in two years. There is material doubt over recoverability of £81m of the council's cash; this is contingent lending to a loss-making entity with uncertain recovery prospects.
findings.figures: £81 million outstanding loan balance, £5 million ECL (increased from £2 million), £61 million Qualis assets vs. debt, £16 million planned write-off in 2027/28, £3.4 million revised carpark valuation (down from £19.4 million in forgiven loans)
findings.quote: Furthermore, we note that as of June 2025 the value of Qualis assets and WIP is £61 million against council lending of £81 million, raising concerns for how these loans will ultimately be repaid.

findings.paper_title: v1 Appendix B - EFDC Final Annual Auditors Report
findings.headline: Disclaimed audit opinion on 2024/25 financial statements — no assurance over opening balances or comparative figures
findings.detail: Following a disclaimed opinion in 2023/24, the auditor cannot provide assurance over brought-forward balances, in-year movements, or prior-year comparatives in the 2024/25 accounts. Material and pervasive misstatement cannot be ruled out. This is EY's first substantive audit of the council and they have stated the disclaimer will likely extend into 2025/26 with continued rebuilding of assurance needed.
findings.matters: A lender cannot verify the council's true financial position or track whether deficits are worsening or improving. The auditor's inability to conclude on going concern is a critical gap.
findings.figures: Disclaimer issued on 2024/25; 2023/24 also disclaimed; unmodified opinion only achieved on 2022/23
findings.quote: As a result of the disclaimer of opinion on the 2023/24 financial statements, we do not have assurance over some brought forward balances from 2023/24 where we did not gain assurance (the opening balances). This means we do not have assurance over all 2024/25 in-year movements and the comparative prior year movements.

findings.paper_title: v1 Appendix A - Epping - Audit result report 2024-25 final
findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease accounting implementation not audited—Council could not provide required lease contracts
findings.detail: The auditor was unable to complete planned procedures on the Council's implementation of IFRS 16 (lease accounting), which became effective from 1 April 2024. The Council could not provide the required underlying lease contracts for audit samples, preventing the auditor from verifying that right-of-use assets and lease liabilities were correctly recognised on the balance sheet.
findings.matters: IFRS 16 requires recognition of previously off-balance-sheet lease obligations; incomplete audit procedures mean the Council's true lease liabilities and right-of-use assets may be misstated, potentially affecting reported solvency and debt ratios.
findings.figures: IFRS 16 effective from 1 April 2024 in local government; 2024/25 is the first year of application
findings.quote: Due to delays in the audit timetable, our planned work on IFRS 16 implementation was rescheduled to the later stages of the audit. For the samples selected, the Council could not provide the required underlying lease contracts.

findings.paper_title: v1 Appendix A - Epping - Audit result report 2024-25 final
findings.headline: Finance team capacity constraints forced two-week audit pause due to delayed working paper delivery
findings.detail: Working papers were requested on 27 June 2025 with a due date of 26 September 2025, but a sizeable portion were not delivered by the deadline. This backlog forced the auditor to pause the audit for two weeks until November 2025. The working papers that were eventually delivered had quality issues, including hardcoded numbers rather than formulas, requiring the auditor to make new requests.
findings.matters: Persistent capacity and quality issues in the finance function delay financial reporting and audit completion, indicate potential control weaknesses, and raise questions about the Council's ability to prepare accurate accounts and respond to other financial management demands.
findings.figures: Two-week audit pause; working papers due 26 September 2025; audit recommenced late November
findings.quote: A sizeable portion of these were not responded to by the due date. Requests then built up quickly once audit work commenced, resulting in a 2 week pause to the audit being required.

findings.paper_title: v1 Appendix A - Epping - Audit result report 2024-25 final
findings.headline: Multiple material audit differences identified, including misstatements exceeding £140,000
findings.detail: The auditor identified numerous misstatements during the audit exceeding £140,000, affecting revenue expenditure, housing benefits, capital accounting, property valuations, borrowings, and creditors. A large number of disclosure misstatements were also detected. Some misstatements have been corrected by management, but others remain uncorrected in the financial statements.
findings.matters: Material misstatements in key balance sheet and revenue accounts indicate control weaknesses or accounting errors that undermine the reliability of the financial statements and the Council's ability to accurately report its financial position.
findings.figures: Greater than £140,000 in identified misstatements across multiple significant accounts
findings.quote: We have identified a number of misstatements greater than £140,000 during the course of our audit impacting the following significant accounts: - Other service expenditure - Housing benefits - Revenue expenditure financed from capital under statute (REFCUS) - Property. Plant and equipment (PPE) additions - Borrowings - Creditors - Disclosures

findings.paper_title: v1 Appendix A - Epping - Audit result report 2024-25 final
findings.headline: Auditor unable to complete key audit procedures on Qualis loans and group consolidation
findings.detail: The auditor was unable to complete planned procedures on the recoverability of Qualis loans because the Council did not provide the expected quality of working papers and supporting evidence within the audit window. Additionally, the auditor obtained no assurance over group consolidation procedures due to an independence issue at the component auditor and lacked capacity to complete the work independently given time constraints.
findings.matters: Critical audit work on the Council's largest external asset (£80.9m in Qualis loans) and group balances remain incomplete, creating further uncertainty about material misstatements and reducing auditor confidence in the financial statements.
findings.figures: 27 February 2026 backstop date; audit commenced 27 June 2025
findings.quote: We have been unable to conclude our planned procedures in relation to recoverability of Qualis loans as the Council has not provided the expected quality of working papers and requested supporting evidences in our allocated audit window.

findings.paper_title: v1 Appendix A - Epping - Audit result report 2024-25 final
findings.headline: Qualis Group subsidiary experiencing financial losses with £80.9m in loans reduced to £39.3m fair value
findings.detail: The Council's subsidiary Qualis Group continues experiencing financial losses. The Council has made loans of £80.9m to Qualis, but these have been written down to a fair value of £39.3m, representing a loss in value of more than £41m. The auditor notes delayed project delivery, ongoing trading losses, and continued reliance on Council funding to sustain operations.
findings.matters: A significant portion of Council assets (loans to the subsidiary) are impaired and may be unrecoverable; the Council faces ongoing funding commitments to a loss-making entity, which constrains its financial flexibility and capacity to meet other obligations or invest in services.
findings.figures: £80.9m loan balance; £39.3m fair value; forecast losses reported in Cabinet Q1 2025/26 reports
findings.quote: Qualis Group Ltd (subsidiary) is experiencing ongoing financial losses, with increased expected credit loss on Council loans and a deteriorating financial position. There is a risk to the recoverability of loans and future financial sustainability if losses persist and further Council financing is required.

findings.paper_title: v1 Appendix A - Epping - Audit result report 2024-25 final
findings.headline: Auditor has disclaimed opinion on 2024/25 financial statements due to insufficient audit evidence
findings.detail: The auditor was unable to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to provide an audit opinion on the Council's 2024/25 financial statements before the 27 February 2026 backstop date. This is compounded by the prior year 2023/24 financial statements also having a disclaimer of opinion, meaning there is no assured opening balance for 2024/25 and no assurance over brought-forward balances.
findings.matters: Lenders cannot rely on audited financial statements to assess the Council's true financial position, liquidity, or solvency; this is a fundamental constraint on credit assessment and removes independent validation of the Council's financial health.
findings.figures: Backstop date 27 February 2026; prior year 2023/24 also disclaimed
findings.quote: we have not been able to complete the detailed audit procedures that would be needed to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence to issue an unmodified audit report on the Group and Council's financial statements for the year ended 31 March 2025

findings.headline: Council relies on £170m commercial property portfolio for 17% of service expenditure, with 2026 valuations estimated pending full revaluation.
findings.detail: The commercial property portfolio (£170.084m as at March 2025) comprises shops (£102.470m) and industrial units (£45.969m), generating net income of £8.935m in 2024/25. Investment income is budgeted at £13.778m for 2026/27, representing 17% of total service expenditure. The March 2026 valuation remains estimated only, pending full revaluation at year-end closure.
findings.matters: A material portion of the council's operating budget depends on maintaining rents and property values. Tenant defaults, commercial property market downturns, or significant valuation write-downs would directly reduce service funding.
findings.figures: Property portfolio £170.084m (shops £102.470m, industrial £45.969m); investment income budget 2026/27 £13.778m representing 17% of £79.833m service expenditure
findings.quote: *31/03/26 valuations estimated only – full valuations to be conducted as part of closure processes.

findings.headline: Council has guaranteed pension liabilities for 63 TUPE-protected employees transferred to Qualis, creating contingent liability if the subsidiary cannot meet LGPS obligations.
findings.detail: The council transferred 38 employees to Qualis in October 2020 (Housing Repairs service) and 25 more in May 2023 (Grounds Maintenance). The council guaranteed their pension costs to Essex County Pension Fund, meaning if Qualis is unable to meet its LGPS liabilities, the General Fund is liable to cover the costs.
findings.matters: This off-balance-sheet contingent liability could crystallise into unexpected General Fund costs, particularly given the credit risk signals from loss allowances on Qualis lending.
findings.figures: 38 employees transferred October 2020 plus 25 transferred May 2023 equals 63 total TUPE-protected employees
findings.quote: The Council also provided a guarantee (to the Essex County Pension Fund) pension costs for 38 'TUPE protected' employees that transferred to Qualis in October 2020

findings.headline: Council must borrow £101.2m over the next three years, with capital financing requirement rising from £382.1m to £407.9m by 2029.
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement is increasing due to its capital programme. It will need to take out £101.2m in new borrowing over 2026/27 to 2028/29. Currently borrowing £276m from PWLB (as at December 2025), it may borrow up to £332.6m in 2026/27 alone if minimum investment levels are achieved.
findings.matters: This significant new borrowing increases the council's total debt burden and debt service costs, affecting leverage ratios and creditworthiness.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Requirement: 2024/25 £382.1m rising to 2028/29 £407.9m; new borrowing required £101.2m over three years; current borrowing £276m
findings.quote: The Council has an increasing CFR due to the Capital Programme and will therefore, be required to take out further (new) borrowing up to £101.2m over the forecast period (2026/27 to 2028/29).

findings.headline: Qualis subsidiary shows credit stress with £4.458m loss allowances set against £51.225m in service loans (8.7% loss rate).
findings.detail: The council has lent £51.225m to Qualis (its housing and economic development subsidiary) across working capital (£3.435m), asset purchase (£11.961m), and development loans (£35.560m). It has set aside £4.458m in loss allowances reflecting expected non-payment. Additionally, the council provided a separate £30m investment loan to Qualis for commercial property acquisition outside the district.
findings.matters: High loss allowance rates indicate material credit risk in the subsidiary. If Qualis cannot service its debt or is in financial distress, the council faces loan losses and loses dividend income that supports its budget.
findings.figures: Qualis service loans £51.225m with loss allowance £4.458m; separate investment loan £30m; total Qualis exposure £81.225m
findings.quote: Accounting standards require the Council to set aside a loss allowance for loans, reflecting the likelihood of non-payment.

findings.headline: Tax base growth assumptions depend on housing delivery; LGR adds forecast uncertainty
findings.detail: Council tax base projections rely on 'average of the last 4 years housing growth'. The paper notes delivery 'will need to be closely monitored'. Pending Local Government Reorganisation clouds the housing pipeline forecast.
findings.matters: If housing growth underperforms, council tax income will fall short, widening the already-identified future-year deficits. LGR uncertainty makes forecasts fragile.
findings.figures: Tax base assumptions based on 4-year housing growth average
findings.quote: The tax base projections used in the MTFP are predicated on the average of the last 4 years housing growth. Delivery will need to be closely monitored to ensure the assumptions remain valid.

findings.headline: Capital programme delivered £15.90m underspend (25% of budget)
findings.detail: Against a £64.39m capital budget in 2025/26, actual outturn forecast is £48.49m, a £15.90m slip. Capital delivery is running 25% behind plan, threatening the asset and income-generation strategies the council depends on.
findings.matters: Slippage reduces both service modernisation pace and anticipated income from capital-funded schemes. Given future-year deficits, capital delivery risk compounds financial pressure.
findings.figures: £15.90m underspend on £64.39m budget
findings.quote: The 2025/26 capital programme totals £64.39m... Spending in the first nine months was £27.87m, with a forecast outturn of £48.49m, resulting in a projected underspend of £15.90m.

findings.headline: Council tax at 2.98% is at the maximum referendum-safe ceiling
findings.detail: The council has set council tax at 2.98%, the maximum allowable without referendum (2.99% assumed by government). Tax-raising capacity is exhausted. The £1.54m and £2.69m future deficits cannot be solved by further council tax rises.
findings.matters: The council has no headroom for tax rises to fund future-year gaps. Deficits must be solved by service cuts or income growth.
findings.figures: 2.98% increase; Band D £177.12 per annum
findings.quote: The Government has assumed in its forecast of Local Authority core spending power that Council Tax will increase by 2.99%.

findings.headline: HRA planned deficits of £5.5m in 2026/27 draw down reserves deliberately
findings.detail: The HRA shows a planned deficit of £5.519m in 2026/27 to utilise surplus reserves due to capital programme reprofiling. This reduces cash buffers for housing operations when demand (repairs, voids, rent arrears) is unpredictable.
findings.matters: Reserves are one-time use. Deliberately running HRA deficits reduces resilience when housing-specific pressures emerge.
findings.quote: Members should note that the planned deficits reflected in the table above represent a deliberate strategy to utilise surplus reserves. These have arisen due to reprofiling of expenditure in the capital programme.

findings.headline: HRA rent increase at 4.8% is the minimum viable level with no flexibility
findings.detail: The council proposes a 4.8% rent increase under the Rent Standard. The paper explicitly states lower increases would add £6.35m to debt over the 30-year plan. The council has no room to absorb cost pressures through rent moderation.
findings.matters: This is a binding constraint. Any HRA cost overrun cannot be absorbed by rent rises; it must be resolved through capital reprioritisation or service cuts.
findings.figures: £6.35m additional debt over 30 years if rents held below 4.8%
findings.quote: An increase of lower than 4.8% would place significant pressure on the HRA with debt being almost £6.35m higher at the end of the 30-year plan.

findings.headline: Homelessness demand escalating despite increased government funding
findings.detail: The council identifies 'the continuing escalation in households presenting as homeless' as an ongoing cost pressure. Despite increased government funding, this 'continues to place significant financial pressure on the authority'. This is a demand-led risk the council cannot fully control.
findings.matters: Homelessness costs are volatile and potentially uncapped. This is an identified pressure where government funding does not fully offset demand growth.
findings.figures: £0.10m additional Homelessness grant for 2026-27 only (implying ongoing demand not fully funded)
findings.quote: the continuing escalation in households presenting as homeless. Despite increased Government funding, this continues to place significant financial pressure on the authority.

findings.headline: Business rates settlement loss of £0.63m from provisional to final
findings.detail: Between the provisional December 2025 settlement and the final settlement in February 2026, the council lost £0.63m due to revised business rates pooling treatment. Further losses of £0.630m and £0.635m follow in subsequent years.
findings.matters: This shows forecasting error on a material income stream. The ongoing losses compound the already-identified future-year deficits.
findings.quote: A revised treatment of Business rates pooling gains. This has resulted in a reduction in the Fair Funding Assessment (in particular revenue support grant), the Recovery guarantee, and the funding floor allocation. Funding has reduced by £0.63m.

findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) grant is volatile and outside core spending power
findings.detail: The council is relying on £1.5m EPR grant for waste services, but this is allocated annually with no certainty. It is explicitly positioned outside 'core spending power', making it an unreliable income source. Any reduction would create immediate budget pressure.
findings.matters: Lenders need to assess true sustainable revenue. Income that 'presents significant uncertainty' and is announced year-to-year cannot be banked reliably.
findings.quote: The Council has been allocated £1.5m for 2026/27, with allocations announced on an annual basis. This funding is outside of core spending power and presents an area of significant uncertainty.

findings.headline: General Fund deficits of £1.54m and £2.69m in 2027/28 and 2028/29 remain unfunded
findings.detail: The council has balanced 2026/27 but explicitly states future-year gaps remain. The problem has been pushed forward, not solved. No detail is provided on how these will be closed beyond vague references to 'maximising technology' and 'exploring income opportunities'.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has genuinely stabilised or is deferring a growing structural deficit that will force either cuts or reserves depletion.
findings.quote: The budget for 2026/27 has been balanced and there remains a deficit in future years of £1.54m in 2027/28 and £2.69m in 2028/29.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates uncertainty over capital and financing strategy
findings.detail: Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) is mentioned multiple times in the strategy as a consideration for medium-term direction. An external review of operational assets was undertaken in 2025/26, but 'further work is currently underway, with the medium term strategic direction being considered within the context of Local Government Reorganisation.' This suggests the council's three-year capital plan may need significant revision depending on LGR outcome.
findings.matters: LGR could alter the council's borrowing authority, merger impacts, or asset transfers, making forward financial projections subject to unknown structural change.
findings.quote: An external review of key operational assets was undertaken during 2025/26. This has provided a high level view of anticipated future maintenance costs, which have been considered as part of the budget process. Further work is currently underway, with the medium term strategic direction being considered within the context of Local Government Reorganisation (LGR).

findings.headline: Substantial HRA borrowing growth with General Fund as guarantor
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account's debt is forecast to grow from £158.4m (2025/26 forecast) to £180.8m (2026/27) and reach £222.9m by 2028/29. The council's legal position is that if the HRA cannot repay debt, the General Fund is liable. This creates a cross-subsidy risk: if HRA rental income or cost assumptions deteriorate, the General Fund must cover the shortfall.
findings.matters: Growing HRA debt guaranteed by the General Fund reduces the General Fund's effective financial resilience and creates a structural risk if housing assumptions prove optimistic.
findings.quote: if the HRA is unable to repay the debt at any point in the future, the Council (through its General Fund) is liable to repay any remaining balance.

findings.headline: Council's financial viability increasingly dependent on commercial property and Qualis performance
findings.detail: The council's Commercial Property Portfolio (£170.084m balance sheet value) and Qualis investments (£35.560m in development loans, plus £51.226m total service investments) together generate 65-67% of the council's net revenue stream income according to the local prudential indicator. The council notes that the standard CIPFA indicator would show 22-26% of financing costs as a share of revenue if this income were lost.
findings.matters: High concentration of income on commercial assets and a single service company (Qualis) creates vulnerability to property valuation drops, void rates, tenant insolvency, or Qualis underperformance.
findings.figures: Total Service and Commercial Investment income: £12.542m (2024/25 actual), forecast £12.404m (2025/26), £13.778m (2026/27); proportion of net revenue stream: 65-67%; Commercial Property portfolio value: £170.084m; Qualis development loans: £35.560m net book value
findings.quote: the relatively high proportion of income from Service and Commercial Investments illustrated in the table above reflects the Council's commercial focus over many years as a means of protecting local public services, whilst maintaining a low Council Tax.

findings.headline: General Fund financing costs nearly doubling as proportion of revenue
findings.detail: General Fund financing costs (interest on debt plus minimum revenue provision) are expected to rise from £2.934m in 2025/26 to £5.242m in 2026/27, with the burden staying elevated at £5.522m (2027/28) and £5.478m (2028/29). As a proportion of the council's local indicator for net revenue stream, this doubles from 9% to 14-15% over the forecast period.
findings.matters: Rapidly rising financing costs reduce the council's headroom for unexpected pressures and constrain service spending; a lender needs confidence this trajectory is sustainable.
findings.figures: Financing Costs (General Fund): £2.934m (2025/26 forecast) → £5.242m (2026/27) → £5.522m (2027/28) → £5.478m (2028/29); as proportion of Net Revenue Stream (Local Indicator): 9% → 14% → 15% → 15%
findings.quote: Proportion of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream (Local Indicator) – financing costs had been rising due to the Council's medium term capital investment ambitions, including its plans for Qualis.

findings.headline: Right to Buy income has collapsed due to national scheme changes
findings.detail: The council's projected capital receipts are falling sharply: £13.885m forecast in 2025/26, dropping to £8.008m in 2026/27, £5.059m in 2027/28, and £1.528m in 2028/29. This is driven primarily by Right to Buy, where national changes with 'significantly reduced discounts to purchasers' mean the council expects 'greatly reduced' disposals going forward. An average of 12 disposals per annum had been assumed historically.
findings.matters: Capital receipts were historically a major funding source; their collapse forces reliance on debt and reserves, tightening the council's financial flexibility.
findings.quote: following national changes to the scheme, which entail significantly reduced discounts to purchasers, expectations have been greatly reduced for disposals over the period of the strategy.

findings.headline: HRA interest cover falling despite planned debt growth
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account's ability to cover interest from net revenue is declining from 1.73 in 2025/26 to 1.35 in 2026/27 and further to 1.31 by 2028/29. The council acknowledges this is because HRA debt is being increased to fund housing capital (£48.864m in 2026/27 alone). While still above the 1.25 minimum threshold, the trajectory is concerning.
findings.matters: Falling interest cover on an expanding HRA debt book is a warning signal for lenders, especially as the council is using HRA income to service growing debt loads.
findings.quote: The projected cover reduces in line with additional funding of the planned housing capital programme.

findings.headline: Debt maturity heavily concentrated in 15-20 year band (37% of borrowing), creating refinancing risk
findings.detail: Of the council's £269.1m borrowing, 37% matures in the 15-20 year window, creating significant refinancing risk in that period. The next largest bucket is 10-15 years (25%). This concentration in mid-to-long-term debt means refinancing risk is deferred but concentrated, leaving the council exposed to whatever interest rate environment prevails in 2040-2045.
findings.matters: A concentrated maturity profile creates cliff risk; if refinancing needs coincide with a rising-rate environment, the council could face material cost pressure. The reliance on investment income makes this more acute if it continues to underperform.
findings.figures: 15-20 years: 37% of borrowing; 10-15 years: 25%; 5-10 years: 24%; other bands all under 7%; weighted average maturity 11.6 years
findings.quote: 15 years and within 20 years 50% 0% 37% Yes

findings.headline: External borrowing increased £15.9m in first half to £269.1m; Capital Financing Requirement forecast to grow to £466m by 2026/27
findings.detail: External borrowing rose from £253.2m (31 March 2025) to £269.1m (30 September 2025), an increase of £15.9m in six months. The Capital Financing Requirement is forecast to grow from £382.1m actual (2024/25) to £435.8m (Q2 forecast 2025/26) to £466.0m (2025/26 budget) to £476.3m (2026/27 budget). This borrowing funds the capital programme and Qualis development projects, including Springwood Grove.
findings.matters: Rapid growth in both actual borrowing and the underlying need to borrow (CFR) signals accelerating capital spend; combined with investment income underperformance, the council is increasing leverage while core revenues miss expectations.
findings.figures: Borrowing increased £15.9m in 6 months; CFR forecast £435.8m (Q2 2025/26), budget £466.0m (2025/26), projected £476.3m (2026/27); PWLB borrowing £269.1m at 3.44% weighted average
findings.quote: Borrowing – external borrowing increased by £15.9 million (from £253.2 million to £269.1 million) during the period April 2025 to September 2025; and...there has been the further rollout of Development Loans to Qualis and funding for the wider Capital Programme.

findings.headline: Commercial property income impacted by tenant renegotiations, raising questions about portfolio resilience
findings.detail: Commercial property portfolio worth £170.1m on the balance sheet has seen recent rent renegotiations with tenants, resulting in income adjustments. While Q2 net income (£4.856m) was slightly up year-on-year (£4.593m in 2024/25), the paper explicitly notes this reflects renegotiation with commercial tenants and observes that 'historically, the Commercial Property portfolio has proved very resilient, but an increase in write-offs cannot be ruled out in the future and this continues to be impacted by the prevailing economic climate.'
findings.matters: Tenant pressure to renegotiate downwards suggests either market softness or wider tenant stress; the council's explicit caveat about future write-off risk signals awareness of potential portfolio weakness.
findings.figures: Commercial property balance sheet value £170.084m; Q2 net income £4.856m vs £4.593m prior year; includes £102.5m in shops, £46m industrial, £21.6m other
findings.quote: The Committee should note that the numbers reflect the accrued position currently in the Council's books, which does not take account of the collectability of income. Historically, the Commercial Property portfolio has proved very resilient, but an increase in write-offs cannot be ruled out in the future and this continues to be impacted by the prevailing economic climate.

findings.headline: Qualis concentration of £82.9m (service loans £52.9m + commercial loan £30m) represents major single-entity exposure
findings.detail: The council holds £52.9m in service investment loans to Qualis (working capital, asset purchase, and development loans for Springwood Grove) plus £30m in a 10-year commercial loan, totalling £82.9m to a single wholly-owned subsidiary. Development loans to Qualis increased by £2.8m in Q2 alone. This concentration is material given that Qualis income is now underperforming budget.
findings.matters: Concentration of this magnitude in a single entity—even if council-owned—creates both revenue risk (as income is now missing targets) and credit risk if Qualis projects underperform or assets decline in value.
findings.figures: Service investments £52.936m (Qualis £52.684m); Commercial loan £30.0m; Development loans increased by £2.803m in quarter
findings.quote: Outstanding Developments Loans to Qualis have increased by £3.5 million during the quarter; this enabled the continued development of Springwood Grove.

findings.headline: Investment income 64% of revenue stream, below the 69% originally expected in Capital Strategy
findings.detail: The Q2 forecast shows investment income as 64% of net revenue stream, down from the 69% expectation in the Capital Strategy. The paper attributes this to 'slightly reduced income expectations from Qualis loans and adjustments to commercial income following recent renegotiations with commercial tenants'. This represents a 5-percentage-point miss against original expectations for the council's main income source.
findings.matters: The council has structured its finances around investment income representing two-thirds of revenue; underperformance of this key income stream indicates either operational stress in Qualis or market pressure on commercial property that may constrain future revenue.
findings.figures: 64% forecast vs 69% Capital Strategy expectation; total investment income £12.529m against net revenue stream
findings.quote: The 64% forecast at Q2 compares to an expectation of 69% in the Capital Strategy. This reflects a combination of slightly reduced income expectations from Qualis loans and adjustments to commercial income following recent renegotiations with commercial tenants.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Treasury Management Quarter 4 Update 2024/25
findings.headline: Council acknowledges collection risk on £170m commercial property portfolio amid weakening economic outlook
findings.detail: The Council holds £170.084m in commercial property investments (shops, industrial units, and other property) which generated £8.935m net income in 2024/25, up from £8.256m the prior year following rent reviews. However, the Council explicitly states that reported accrued income does not account for collectability and flags material write-off risk in the current economic environment, despite the portfolio's historical resilience during the pandemic.
findings.matters: Commercial property income is a material and growing component of council cash flow; significant tenant defaults or asset impairments would impact both revenue sustainability and balance sheet solvency. The acknowledgment of collection risk in a weakening economy signals this is actively being monitored as a concern.
findings.figures: Commercial property balance sheet value £170.084m (Shops £102.470m, Industrial Units £45.969m, Other £21.645m); 2024/25 net income £8.935m (2023/24: £8.256m); includes unexpected Business Rates charge at former HMRC site
findings.quote: The Committee should note that the numbers reflect the accrued position currently in the Council's books, which does not take account of the collectability of income. The Commercial Property portfolio proved very resilient during the pandemic, but an increase in write-offs cannot be ruled out in the future given the current economic climate.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Treasury Management Quarter 4 Update 2024/25
findings.headline: Capital financing strategy dependent on depleting one-off land sale proceeds; structural funding gap emerging
findings.detail: The Council received substantial proceeds from the December 2023 North Weald Airfield land disposal and has used these to fund capital expenditure instead of new PWLB borrowing. Investment balances have fallen from £43.9m to £13.6m (a 69% reduction) in a single year as this cash is deployed. Simultaneously, the General Fund CFR has jumped 21% from £188.9m to £228.5m, while external borrowing has increased only £0.1m. By March 2026, the Council's own Liability Benchmark forecasts a CFR of £470.4m and minimum borrowing requirement of £363.1m, yet the Council is planning to borrow only £261.1m—a gap of £102m that will need to be funded from other sources (reserves, further asset sales, or revised borrowing plans) when North Weald proceeds are exhausted.
findings.matters: This is an explicitly temporary funding strategy that will require a material transition to higher borrowing or equivalent reserve drawdowns within 12-18 months, fundamentally altering the Council's debt and liquidity position. A lender needs to understand the sustainability plan for this transition.
findings.figures: General Fund CFR £188.906m to £228.482m (+21%); Total CFR £343.531m to £382.078m (+£38.5m); Investments £43.9m to £13.6m (-69%); Internal borrowing £90.479m to £116.955m (+29%); Liability Benchmark 31/03/26 £363.1m vs planned borrowing £261.1m; net borrowing increased £30.5m to £239.7m (+14.6%)
findings.quote: further long-term PWLB borrowing has been minimised in 2024/25 due to the availability of cash balances following the land disposal at North Weald Airfield in December 2023

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Treasury Management Quarter 1 Update 2025/26
findings.headline: External borrowing increased by £12.82 million in Q1 to fund capital programme and Qualis development
findings.detail: Total external borrowing rose from £253.2m to £266.0m in the three months to 30 June 2025. The increase was specifically drawn to fund the wider capital programme and completion of existing Qualis projects. The Capital Financing Requirement is forecast to rise from £382m to £441m by March 2026.
findings.matters: This shows accelerating capital and development spending funded by borrowing. Lenders need visibility on why borrowing is rising, the sustainability of the capital programme, and the council's capacity to service increasing debt.
findings.figures: Borrowing increased £12.82m to £266.0m; CFR forecast to increase to £441.271m by 31 March 2026 (from £382.078m)
findings.quote: Borrowing – external borrowing increased by £12.82 million (from £253.2 million to £266.0 million) during the period April 2025 to June 2025

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Treasury Management Quarter 1 Update 2025/26
findings.headline: Commercial property portfolio at risk of increased write-offs due to economic conditions
findings.detail: The council holds £170.084m in commercial property investments (shops, industrial units, and other assets) generating £2.339m net income in Q1. The paper explicitly states that while the portfolio has historically been resilient, write-offs cannot be ruled out and performance is being impacted by the prevailing economic climate.
findings.matters: A £170m portfolio with acknowledged collectability risks and economic headwinds could see income disruption if tenants fail or rents cannot be collected. This affects the council's revenue position and its ability to service debt.
findings.figures: Commercial Property balance sheet value £170.084m; Q1 2025/26 net income £2.339m (compared to £2.306m prior year)
findings.quote: The Committee should note that the numbers reflect the accrued position currently in the Council's books, which does not take account of the collectability of income. Historically, the Commercial Property portfolio has proved very resilient, but an increase in write-offs cannot be ruled out in the future and this continues to be impacted by the prevailing economic climate.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Treasury Management Quarter 1 Update 2025/26
findings.headline: £30 million commercial loan to Qualis has no Minimum Revenue Provision despite 10-year maturity
findings.detail: A £30m loan to Qualis (maturing September 2030) is being charged with no MRP despite accounting policy normally requiring it. The council's protection is limited to a floating charge on the underlying commercial assets purchased with the loan proceeds.
findings.matters: This is an unusual arrangement that deviates from standard practice. MRP ensures loans are repaid over their life; without it, there is no systematic repayment profile, and the council relies entirely on the asset value holding and Qualis's ability to repay at maturity.
findings.figures: Qualis Investment Loan balance £30.0m, 10-year maturity September 2030
findings.quote: Members should note that, in accordance with the Council's MRP Policy and the prevailing accounting rules at the point at which the Commercial Loan to Qualis was granted (in September 2020), MRP is not provided on this loan. However, the Council has purposely protected its position in the form of a 'floating charge' on the underlying commercial assets that were purchased (by Qualis) with the proceeds from the loan.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 for Treasury Management Quarter 1 Update 2025/26
findings.headline: Development loans to Qualis subsidiary increased by £3.5 million in one quarter
findings.detail: Outstanding development loans to Qualis (the council's wholly-owned subsidiary) rose from £35.56m to £39.06m in Q1 2025/26 alone, funding the Springwood Grove development. Total exposure to Qualis across working capital, asset purchase, and development loans is £54.605m.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's concentrated exposure to subsidiary lending, particularly for speculative property development. This is commercial risk sitting on the council's balance sheet.
findings.figures: Development Loans increased £3.5m to £39.06m; total Qualis service investments £54.605m
findings.quote: Outstanding Developments Loans to Qualis have increased by £3.5 million during the quarter; this enabled the continued development of Springwood Grove.
